hints: Think about where ionic character is strongest in Period 3, on the left where metals lose electrons easily to chlorine.
walkthrough:
Sort metals from non-metals**
Sodium and magnesium are strongly metallic elements on the left of Period 3. They transfer electrons to chlorine to form $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions with $\text{Cl}^-$ ions in a giant lattice. The chlorides further right become increasingly covalent.
Final answer: $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$

hints: Recall which Period 3 chlorides hydrolyse completely to release $\text{HCl}$ fumes and give very low pH, rather than just dissolving.
walkthrough:
Link covalent character to hydrolysis**
The highly charged or electron deficient covalent chlorides react vigorously with water. $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ all hydrolyse to give $\text{HCl(aq)}$ and a strongly acidic solution with white fumes.
Final answer: $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$

hints: Decide which chloride simply separates into hydrated ions in water without reacting with water to release $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Pick the chloride that does not hydrolyse**
$\text{NaCl}$ is a Group 1 ionic solid. In water it just dissociates into hydrated $\text{Na}^+(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})$. Neither ion reacts with water, so the solution stays neutral at pH 7. $\text{MgCl}_2$ slightly hydrolyses to give a weakly acidic solution.

hints: Recall the melting point pattern across Period 3 elements, which element forms a giant covalent lattice with very strong bonds.
walkthrough:
Find the highest melting Period 3 element**
Across Na to Ar, melting point rises to a maximum at silicon. Silicon has a giant covalent tetrahedral network with many strong $\text{Si-Si}$ bonds to break, so it melts far higher than metals like Na and Mg or simple molecular $\text{P}$, $\text{S}$, $\text{Cl}$. Its chloride is therefore $\text{SiCl}_4$.

hints: Remember chlorine with cold dilute alkali disproportionates to oxidation states -1 and +1, think bleach.
walkthrough:
Write the disproportionation**
With cold aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, $\text{Cl}_2$ is both oxidised and reduced:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Since $\text{NaCl}$ is already given, the other products are sodium chlorate(I), $\text{NaClO}$, and water.
Final answer: $\text{NaClO}$ / sodium chlorate(I) / sodium hypochlorite and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Focus on what happens to the $\text{-OH}$ group when $\text{PCl}_5$ acts, the $\text{OH}$ is swapped for another atom.
walkthrough:
Spot the swap**
The $\text{-OH}$ group of the alcohol is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ to give a chloroalkane plus $\text{POCl}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$. Replacing one group by another is substitution.

hints: Draw butane-1,3-diol as $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ and remember excess $\text{PCl}_5$ will react at every $\text{OH}$ site.
walkthrough:
Replace both OH groups**
Butane-1,3-diol is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$. With excess $\text{PCl}_5$, both $\text{-OH}$ groups are substituted by $\text{-Cl}$. You get $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Cl)CH}_3$, which is 1,3-dichlorobutane, shown as $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ when drawn reversed.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ / 1,3-dichlorobutane: $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{C(H)(Cl)}-\text{C(H)(H)}-\text{C(H)(H)}-\text{Cl}$

hints: Use the physical clue first, what does being a liquid at room temperature tell you about structure compared to a giant lattice.
Use the chemical clue next, which type of bonding in chlorides allows vigorous reaction with water to give an acidic solution.
walkthrough:
Read the liquid clue**
A cherry red liquid means melting and boiling points are low. Giant ionic or giant covalent lattices need huge energy to break strong lattices, so they are solids. A liquid must be simple molecular, with only weak London or dipole forces between separate $\text{SCl}_2$ molecules.

Read the hydrolysis clue**
Ionic chlorides like $\text{NaCl}$ just dissolve. Covalent chlorides hydrolyse to release $\text{HCl}$. Since $\text{SCl}_2$ reacts vigorously with water to form an acidic solution, its bonding must be covalent.

Final answer: Structure is simple / molecular as $\text{SCl}_2$ has low melting / boiling point, only weak intermolecular forces to overcome.
Bonding is covalent as $\text{SCl}_2$ is hydrolysed by water to give acidic solution.

hints: Combine reaction 1 and reaction 2 by Hess Law so that $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$ cancels to give the formation of $\text{SCl}_2$ from $\text{S}_8$ and $\text{Cl}_2$.
Set up the enthalpy sum for $8\text{SCl}_2$ then divide by 8, watching the stoichiometry: $\Delta H = \Delta H_{r1} + 4\Delta H_{r2}$.
walkthrough:
Build the Hess cycle**
Reaction 1 makes $4\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$ from $\text{S}_8 + 4\text{Cl}_2$. Reaction 2 converts $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2 + \text{Cl}_2$ to $2\text{SCl}_2$. To get rid of all $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$, multiply reaction 2 by 4 and add:
$$\text{S}_8 + 8\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 8\text{SCl}_2$$
Enthalpy for this overall route is:
$$\Delta H = -58.2 + 4(-40.6) = -58.2 - 162.4 = -220.8\ \text{kJ}$$.

Scale to one mole**
Formation enthalpy is for 1 mol of $\text{SCl}_2(\text{l})$ from elements in standard states. Divide by 8:
$$\Delta H_{f} = \frac{-220.8}{8} = -27.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Final answer: By Hess Law: $\Delta H_{r1} + 4\Delta H_{r2} = 8\Delta H_{f}(\text{SCl}_2)$
$(-58.2) + 4(-40.6) = -220.8 = 8\Delta H_{f}$
$\Delta H_{f} = -27.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Count moles of gas on each side of reaction 2, remembering liquids do not count for pressure effects.
walkthrough:
Count gases only**
In reaction 2, $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2(\text{l}) + \text{Cl}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SCl}_2(\text{l})$, there is 1 mol of gas on the left and 0 mol of gas on the right. Lower pressure favours the side with more gas molecules, so equilibrium shifts left to make more $\text{Cl}_2$.
Final answer: Equilibrium moves to left as there are more moles of gas on left hand side.

hints: Start your definition with what isomers always share, the atoms present.
Then state what is different about how those atoms are joined together.
walkthrough:
Same formula**
Structural isomers contain exactly the same number and type of atoms, so $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$ in both isomer I and II has the same molecular formula.

Different structure**
What differs is how the atoms are linked. In isomer I the connectivity is $\text{Cl-S-S-Cl}$, in isomer II it is $\text{S=SCl}_2$. Different structural formula from the same molecular formula is the definition.
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae / different arrangement of atoms / different connectivity.

hints: Count electron domains on the S bonded to Cl in isomer I, how many bonding pairs and lone pairs surround it.
Recall how lone pair repulsion compresses the tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$ and what range this gives for two lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Find the electron pairs**
Look at either S in $\text{Cl-S-S-Cl}$. Each S forms two single bonds, one to Cl and one to S, and sulfur in Group 16 brings 6 outer electrons. After sharing 2, 4 remain as 2 lone pairs. So you have 4 electron domains, tetrahedral arrangement of electron pairs.

Apply lone pair squeeze**
Lone pair to lone pair repulsion is strongest and squeezes bonding pairs together. With two lone pairs the $\text{Cl-S-S}$ angle drops well below $109.5^{\circ}$, similar to water at $104.5^{\circ}$ but can be even smaller due to larger S atoms. Any value above $90^{\circ}$ up to about $108^{\circ}$ is accepted.

Final answer: Bond angle $90^{\circ} < \text{Cl-S-S} \leqslant 108^{\circ}$ (accept approx $90^{\circ}$ to $104.5^{\circ}$).
Each S has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, lone pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair repulsion so angle is compressed below $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Identify the bonds in isomer II from Fig. 3.1, one $\text{S=S}$ double bond and two $\text{S-Cl}$ single bonds on the central S.
Work out lone pairs left over, central S has one lone pair and terminal S has two lone pairs, each Cl has three lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Place the shared pairs**
Draw central S joined to two Cl atoms by single bonds and to the top S by a double bond. That is 2 electrons shared in each $\text{S-Cl}$ bond and 4 electrons shared in $\text{S=S}$. Use dots for S electrons and crosses for Cl electrons, or vice versa, to show origin.

Add the lone pairs**
Complete octets: each Cl needs 6 non-bonding electrons (3 pairs). The top S already shares 4 electrons so needs 4 non-bonding electrons (2 lone pairs). The central S shares 8 electrons in total (2+2+4) so with its 6 outer electrons it has 2 electrons left (1 lone pair). Show all outer shell electrons only.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross showing central S double bonded to top S (4 shared electrons) and single bonded to two Cl atoms (2 shared electrons each). Central S has 1 lone pair, terminal S has 2 lone pairs, each Cl has 3 lone pairs. All outer shell electrons shown with correct dots and crosses.
